name: India: Size and Location
summary: Where India sits and how large it looms: a country of the Northern and Eastern hemispheres cut by the Tropic of Cancer, its clocks set to one meridian though the sun rises two hours apart across it, the seventh largest land ringed by neighbours and commanding the Indian Ocean's routes.

questions.stem: India lies entirely north of the equator and east of the prime meridian, with a great line of latitude passing almost through its middle. In which hemispheres does it sit, and which line halves it?
questions.solution: India lies in the Northern and Eastern hemispheres, and the Tropic of Cancer (about 23½°N) passes through the middle of the country, dividing it into roughly equal northern and southern halves. That is the fact this question turns on.

questions.stem: When the sun is rising over Arunachal Pradesh in India's far east, watches in Gujarat in the far west still read about two hours earlier in the day — yet both states keep exactly the same clock time. How can this be, and why is one standard meridian used?
choices: India spans about 30° of longitude, and every 15° equals one hour of the sun's apparent journey, so sunrise really is about two hours apart across the country; to avoid two zones confusing trains and offices, one central meridian (82°30'E) fixes a single Indian Standard Time for all
The sun physically moves faster over eastern India than western India
Gujarat and Arunachal are at the same longitude, so there is no real time gap
India uses a different clock in every state, changing at each border
questions.solution: The two-hour gap is real and comes straight from India's east–west size. The Earth turns once — 360° — in twenty-four hours, so the sun appears to sweep 15° of longitude every hour. India's mainland stretches from about 68°E in the west to about 97°E in the east, close to 30° of longitude, so the sun reaches the eastern edge roughly two hours before the western: dawn genuinely breaks over Arunachal Pradesh long before it does over Gujarat. If each place simply used its own local sun-time, a train crossing the country would have to reset its clock continuously, and timetables, offices and broadcasts would be chaos. To prevent this, India picks one central line of longitude, 82°30'E (passing near Mirzapur), and declares the local time along it to be Indian Standard Time for the entire country. Everyone sets their clocks to that single meridian, even though it means the eastern regions see the sun 'too early' by the clock and the western regions 'too late'. The trade-off is deliberate: a little mismatch with the local sun in exchange for one shared time that keeps a country 3,000 km wide running together. Large countries like the USA or Russia instead choose several time zones; India, valuing simplicity and unity, keeps just one.

questions.stem: India's north–south and east–west distances are almost equal in kilometres (about 3,200 km and 2,900 km), yet the country spans nearly 30° of longitude but only about 29° of latitude in a way that does not match those kilometres neatly. Why do equal-looking distances correspond to such different numbers of degrees?
choices: Lines of latitude stay a roughly constant distance apart everywhere, but lines of longitude are farthest apart at the equator and squeeze together toward the poles; India lies well north of the equator, so each degree of longitude there covers fewer kilometres than a degree of latitude does
The Earth is flat, so degrees and kilometres never match
India is simply measured wrongly in one direction
Degrees of latitude and longitude are always exactly the same size everywhere on Earth
questions.solution: The key is that degrees of latitude and degrees of longitude do not measure the same ground distance, and only latitude behaves simply. Lines of latitude (parallels) are true parallels — they stay a nearly constant distance apart from the equator to the poles — so one degree of latitude is always about 111 km, anywhere on Earth. Lines of longitude (meridians) are different: they all meet at the two poles and spread farthest apart at the equator. So a degree of longitude is worth about 111 km only at the equator, and shrinks as you move toward either pole, following the cosine of the latitude. India sits well north of the equator (roughly 8° to 37°N), so across it a degree of longitude covers noticeably fewer kilometres than a degree of latitude — very roughly 90–100 km against 111 km. That is why India's east–west span can be nearly 30° of longitude and yet cover slightly fewer kilometres than its north–south span of about 29° of latitude: the eastern degrees are 'narrower' on the ground. The lesson is that a map's grid is not a plain ruler — the same number of degrees means a shorter real distance in longitude the farther you are from the equator, which is exactly why shapes look stretched near the poles on a flat world map.
